introduction: The Bahá’í writings say two things about wealth, and this guide keeps both in view. Wealth is “a mighty barrier” and the rich enter with difficulty; and wealth honestly earned and spent for others is “praiseworthy in the highest degree.” Everyone must work, begging is condemned, the poor are “God’s trust” and must be provided for, and giving is to be free and never forced. From that practical ground the readings pass to the instability of possessions, to contentment, and to another kind of riches, which the poor may have and the wealthy lack. Scripture has spoken in both ways before. The Gospels and James are hard on the rich; Proverbs and Ben Sira honour diligence and the blameless rich man; the Qur’án condemns hoarding and praises spending; the law of Moses legislates for the poor. Seneca, Shakespeare, Goldsmith, Ruskin and Dickens add their testimony. The awkward questions are asked through Adam Smith, Carnegie, Wilde, Aristotle and Marx: whether contentment excuses want, whether accumulation is always unjust, whether poverty should be abolished or consoled, and whether talk of spiritual riches is an opiate.
questions: “Wealth is a mighty barrier” and “wealth is praiseworthy in the highest degree.” State the conditions under which each sentence is true.
Begging is condemned, and the poor are “God’s trust among you.” What system of responsibilities do the first two stretches describe, for the individual, the wealthy and the community?
Sharing is to be voluntary. The first Christians held all things in common, and modern states tax. Where do the Bahá’í writings place the line between what love gives and what law requires?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá praises the happiness of a barefoot man in Baghdad and of the Bedouin. Adam Smith says no society is happy whose majority is poor. How do you honour contentment without excusing deprivation?
“Grieve not because of poverty, for verily thou art rich.” Who may say this to whom? What must the speaker also be doing for Marx’s charge of opium to fail?

“All the tyranny and injustice in the world comes from accumulation,” and yet differences in livelihood are called a requirement of wisdom. What kind of economic difference do the readings accept, and what kind do they call injustice?

outside.why: “Wealth is a mighty barrier between the seeker and his desire.” Jesus: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.
The rich young man who had kept every commandment: he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions.

“Neither poverty nor wealth are … praiseworthy or blameworthy until the results of each are seen.” Agur’s prayer in Proverbs: give me neither poverty nor riches; lest I be full, and deny thee; or lest I be poor, and steal.

“Wealth is praiseworthy in the highest degree” if honestly gained and spent for others. Ben Sira: blessed is the rich that is found without blemish, and hath not gone after gold. Who is he? and we will call him blessed.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá praises the wealthy person who spends on schools, industry and the welfare of the people. Andrew Carnegie made that a rule for millionaires and added a sentence on those who do not: the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced. Carnegie made his fortune first, by methods his workers resented. Does the praise in this reading depend on how the wealth was made?

One whom nothing keeps from God may use the earth’s ornaments without harm. The First Letter to Timothy: charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches; that they be rich in good works.
The poor “are God’s trust among you.” Deuteronomy: thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother: but thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him.
Proverbs: he that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord.
A monthly sum for the helpless, and homes for the incapacitated. The law of Moses built provision into the harvest: thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger.
Franklin Roosevelt in 1937: the test of our progress is not whether we add more to the abundance of those who have much; it is whether we provide enough for those who have too little.
The poor of every nation and religion came to ‘Abdu’l-Bahá before he sailed. Jesus: when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind.
“It is indeed good to possess riches if they be expended … to help the orphaned, the poor.” A rich tax collector at Jesus’ table: behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor.
Wealth acquired “through crafts or professions is commendable.” Proverbs: the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
“Blessed is he who beareth burdens but causeth none to bear his own.” Paul: if any would not work, neither should he eat.
Commerce and crafts “are not impediments to serving the Divine Unity.” Paul paid his way: by their occupation they were tentmakers.
Riches earned “with divine assistance.” Moses: thou shalt remember the Lord thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth.
“The most despised of men … are those who sit idly and beg.” Proverbs: go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.
Begging is abhorred, and “the station of the patient among the poor is great.” James: hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom?

“No deed is more abhorrent than begging.” Jesus used asking as his picture of prayer and never scorned the asker: ask, and it shall be given you. Beggars sat at every gate he passed. What is Bahá’u’lláh condemning: need, or a way of life, or a claim made “in the name of Truth”?
“Blessed is the poor one who is patient.” Luke’s beatitude: blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God.
The once wealthy who have fallen into poverty. Job, on the day it happened to him: naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither.
Sharing in the divine teachings is voluntary. Paul: every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.

Equality is by free will, never by compulsion. The first church went further than giving: they had all things common, and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need. Many since have tried to make that a law. Why does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá insist on the voluntary, and what does he add elsewhere by way of law and tax?
Bahá’u’lláh quotes the Qur’án on hoarding. The verse: they who hoard up gold and silver and spend it not in the way of Allah, unto them give tidings of a painful doom.
Spend of what God has given: “thereby will that which ye possess increase.” Proverbs: there is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; the liberal soul shall be made fat.
The Qur’án: the likeness of those who spend their wealth in Allah’s way is as the likeness of a grain which groweth seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains.
“The best of all is the rich-giver.” Jesus watched the treasury and chose another: this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury.
Wealth is good for the hour of service; “otherwise what good is it?” A saying of Jesus preserved by Paul: it is more blessed to give than to receive.

A man worth three hundred millions who never spent on the poor. Jesus: there was a certain rich man, which fared sumptuously every day: and there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate.
Marley’s ghost, too late: mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business.
The treasures of kings are not worth mention; “a grain of mustard offered by His loved ones will be extolled.” Jesus: she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had.
“A person is known by his courteous behavior, not by his wealth.” Burns: the rank is but the guinea’s stamp, the man’s the gold for all that.
Today neither poverty nor wealth, lineage nor strength is regarded. Proverbs: the rich and poor meet together: the Lord is the maker of them all.
Most who sit at the table are the poor. Jesus’ parable of a supper whose invited guests sent excuses: bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind.
“How many souls whose wealth … did not prevent them.” Zacchaeus was chief among the publicans, and he was rich, and he climbed a tree to see.
Wealth prevented one servant and was spent in the path by another. Jesus: ye cannot serve God and mammon.
“Material favors sometimes deprive us of spiritual favors.” Jesus: the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word.
Neither hampered by wealth nor dejected by poverty: “this is a human perfection.” Paul: I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound.
“In spite of poverty he acquires a sense of affluence.” Iago speaks a truth he does not live by: poor and content is rich and rich enough.
“Should prosperity befall thee, rejoice not, and should abasement come upon thee, grieve not.” Kipling: if you can meet with Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same.
“Tonight they are yours, tomorrow others will possess them.” Jesus’ rich farmer: this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be?
A fortune passes to people its owner despised. Ecclesiastes: riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt; he shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand.
“One and all they leave behind them all that is theirs.” The First Letter to Timothy: we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.
“Every treasure hath been … the cause of infinite grief.” The same letter: the love of money is the root of all evil; they have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
“Even this earth’s happiness does not depend upon wealth.” Ecclesiastes: he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver.
Kings with flowing treasuries “pass their days in regret and sorrow.” Henry IV, sleepless: uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.
“Contentment and ease are better than wealth and trouble.” Proverbs: better is little with the fear of the Lord than great treasure and trouble therewith.
Happiness lies “in freedom of spirit, nobility, and the perfections of human reality.” Jesus: a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
John Ruskin, to the economists of his day: there is no wealth but life.
“When one is contented he does not care either for riches or poverty.” Seneca: it is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
In the West, “the more they have of comfort and riches, the more” they want. Wordsworth: getting and spending, we lay waste our powers.

The Bedouin “had often not enough to eat” and were happy. Adam Smith would not have a philosophy of contentment rest on other people’s hunger: no society can surely be flourishing and happy, of which the far greater part of the members are poor and miserable. Where in this guide does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá say the same?
A bird is content with a few grains, “never thinking about supper.” Jesus: behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns.

“How many are they who, though rich in dinars, are yet the poorest of God’s creatures.” Proverbs: there is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches.
“The people have been deluded by their wealth.” The Qur’án: rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you until ye come to the graves.
“Beware lest wealth hold thee back.” The Qur’án: your wealth and your children are only a temptation, whereas Allah! with Him is an immense reward.

“With fire We test the gold, and with gold We test Our servants.” The First Letter of Peter: the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire.
Without faith “wealth causes the hearts to be hardened.” Moses: when thou hast eaten and art full, beware that thou forget not the Lord thy God.
He grew rich and forgot, lost all and repented. The letter to Laodicea: thou sayest, I am rich, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor.
“These possessions will become a burden and this wealth a curse.” James: go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you. Your riches are corrupted.
“Neither their wealth nor their children shall avail them.” Proverbs: riches profit not in the day of wrath.
Millions spent on collections that “produce no result.” Jesus: lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá cites the camel and the needle as Christ’s testimony to “the exaltation of the poor ones.” James to congregations that seated the rich in front: have not the faith with respect of persons.
“The hope of the rich is in their wealth, but the trust of the poor is in God.” A psalm: some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the Lord our God.
“All the tyranny and injustice in the world comes from accumulation.” Oliver Goldsmith in 1770: ill fares the land, to hastening ills a prey, where wealth accumulates, and men decay.
Isaiah to the elders and princes: the spoil of the poor is in your houses. What mean ye that ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor?

Accumulation is the root of injustice. Adam Smith saw in the pursuit of private gain the ordinary engine of everyone’s dinner: it is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. Can both be true? What separates trade from “accumulation”?
A poor Arab in Baghdad, barefoot in a tattered coat, and happy. Paul: as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.

“If all were rich, there would be no opportunity for the appearance of generosity.” Oscar Wilde thought that a bad reason to keep the poor: the proper aim is to try and reconstruct society on such a basis that poverty will be impossible. Is ‘Abdu’l-Bahá defending poverty here, or describing degrees that would remain when destitution is gone?
“God did not create man poor.” A psalm: I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.

Poverty is only a lack, and no part of creation’s design. Deuteronomy seems resigned to it: the poor shall never cease out of the land. The same verse goes on: therefore I command thee, open thine hand wide. What follows in practice from calling poverty an absence?
“Thoughts of wealth and riches … are sheer illusion,” given only that the world might prosper. The Preacher, who had tried wealth to its limit: vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
Bahá’u’lláh did not refuse relief, and his court was “far above such material benefits.” Jesus: the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
The friends are afflicted with destitution. Paul of the churches of Macedonia: their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality.
On the divine path “the wealthy become poor, not the poor wealthy.” Paul: though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
A friend’s bankruptcy is welcomed as fellowship with those long bankrupt for God. Paul: I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ.
One would hope that “grinding poverty” would increase a believer’s joy. Habakkuk: although there shall be no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in the Lord.

Joy in want is asked of the poor man himself. Scripture asks something else of everyone around him: he that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor. When is it right to tell a person in poverty to be thankful, and who may say it?
A teacher travelling “in hunger and in thirst, unclothed and poor” is the embodiment of wealth. Jesus sent out seventy: carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes.
He wishes the believers prosperity without attachment. The Qur’án on the mean between: let not thy hand be chained to thy neck nor open it with a complete opening.
“Were it not for poverty, the light of detachment would not shine forth.” Jesus: blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Muḥammad’s “poverty is my glory” is need of God and wealth in everything else. Rábi‘a: Thou art enough for me.
“Whoso loveth Me is the possessor of all things.” The shepherd psalm: the Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
“True sovereignty must be a treasury of the soul.” Jesus: the kingdom of God is within you.
“Although the blessed purse is empty, there should be a treasure in the sleeve.” Peter to a beggar at the temple gate: silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee.
“The treasure of the Kingdom floweth freely.” Jesus: where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Hardship here, rest in the divine realm. Paul: our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.
A treasure in which “there is no loss or damage.” Proverbs: wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it.
Gold and silver “become the cause of increasing need.” Haggai: he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.
Isaiah: wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not?
The near ones “have ever, in this earthly realm, been sanctified and detached from wealth.” The Letter to the Hebrews: they confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
“The rich of the earth are destitute in the presence of the friends.” Hannah’s song: he raiseth up the poor out of the dust, to set them among princes.
“I created thee rich, why dost thou bring thyself down to poverty?” A psalm: thou hast crowned him with glory and honour.
“Though you may be poor here, you are rich in the treasures of the Kingdom.” The letter to the church at Smyrna: I know thy poverty, but thou art rich.

“Be not grieved on account of poverty for true wealth is surging.” This is the kind of sentence Marx had in mind: religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature; it is the opium of the people. Read the first stretch of this guide again. What in it keeps the consolation from being an opiate?
“The highest form of wealth is your faith in God.” Jesus: this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God.
He who is deprived of it is poor “though he possess all the treasures of the earth.” Jesus: what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
Wealth and exaltation are “in the grasp of God’s power. He giveth and He withholdeth.” Job: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away.
A prayer to the “Enricher of the poor.” Mary: he hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away.

“The wisdom of God necessitates diversity and distinction in the earning of livelihood.” Aristotle accepted difference and feared its extremes: the best political community is formed by citizens of the middle class. How much difference do the Bahá’í teachings accept, and where do they set limits?

james-go-to-now-ye-rich-men.text: Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you. Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten. Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days. Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth

psalm-not-seen-the-righteous-forsaken.text: I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread

proverbs-maketh-himself-poor-yet-hath-gr.text: There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches

ecclesiastes-riches-kept-to-their-hurt.text: There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand. As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand

luke-life-consisteth-not-in-abundance.text: Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth

corinthians-for-your-sakes-he-became-poo.text: For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich

revelation-thy-poverty-but-thou-art-rich.text: I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich

quran-wealth-and-children-only-a-temptat.text: Your wealth and your children are only a temptation, whereas Allah! with Him is an immense reward.

quran-devil-promiseth-you-destitution.text: The devil promiseth you destitution and enjoineth on you lewdness. But Allah promiseth you forgiveness from Himself with bounty. Allah is All-Embracing, All-knowing.

sirach-blessed-is-the-rich-found-without.text: Blessed is the rich that is found without blemish, and hath not gone after gold. Who is he? and we will call him blessed: for wonderful things hath he done among his people. Who hath been tried thereby, and found perfect? then let him glory. Who might offend, and hath not offended? or done evil, and hath not done it? His goods shall be established, and the congregation shall declare his alms

shakespeare-poor-and-content-is-rich.text: Poor and content is rich and rich enough, / But riches fineless is as poor as winter / To him that ever fears he shall be poor
shakespeare-poor-and-content-is-rich.author: William Shakespeare
